qa.a: Disha grew concerned, sensing that one sentence had crowded out the rest of a good review, though Disha couldn't be sure what Pradeep was thinking.

qa.q: How did Disha help Pradeep see the full review?
qa.a: Disha asked Pradeep to read the whole review aloud and then asked what else it said, letting him find the praise himself.

qa.q: How did the review seem to feel to Pradeep before he reread it?
qa.a: It seemed to feel like a warning; the one line about documentation filtered out the praise, so he feared being fired.

grounding: A team lead watches an employee fix on one line of a good review and has him read the whole page aloud and say what else it says.

passage:
Monday. Salma's review meeting with Dhruv went well by every measure: strong code quality, helpful to juniors, praised by two clients. One line said his estimates ran optimistic. Dhruv thanked her and left without another word. Through the glass, she saw him staring at the page for twenty minutes.
Tuesday. At 8 a.m. he emailed: 'Sorry my estimates have been a problem. Should I step back from the release?' Salma called him in, laid the review between them and read it aloud, line by line. Then she asked, 'What does the rest of it say?' He was quiet, then read the praise back to her, haltingly.
Friday. At stand-up Dhruv gave his estimate for the new feature and added, 'Plus a day of buffer, per my review.' Everyone laughed, and so did he.

qa.q: What did the one critical line say about Dhruv?
qa.a: It said his estimates ran optimistic.

qa.q: What did Salma feel when she saw Dhruv staring at the page through the glass?
qa.a: She felt concerned and uneasy, sensing he was fixed on one line of a good review.

qa.q: Why did Salma ask 'What does the rest of it say?'
qa.a: It made Dhruv read the praise for himself, balancing the one criticism instead of just being told not to worry.

qa.q: How did the review look to Dhruv on Monday?
qa.a: It seemed to feel like a failing mark to him; the estimate line filled his view, so he even offered to step back from the release.

grounding: Over a week, a team lead notices an employee fixating on one line of a good review, reads the page aloud with him, and sees him regain balance.

passage: Farida, you asked how I survived my first week running the kitchen. I'll tell you about Thursday. We had forty covers, my biggest night yet, and one table sent back the fish, overcooked. I could feel the whole night collapsing into that one plate. I'm Harsha, I've cooked since I was fifteen, and I still wanted to hide in the cold room. Instead I grabbed an order slip and made two columns. Left side: the dal sold out; the new cook plated fast without mistakes; two tables asked to meet the chef. Right side: fish overcooked, table six. I looked at both. Then I decided: one person would own the fish station on busy nights, with a timer. That was it. The fish was real. So were the other three. You need both columns to know what to fix.

qa.q: How many covers did the kitchen have on Thursday?
qa.a: The kitchen had forty covers.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling when the fish came back?
qa.a: Harsha felt a rush of embarrassment and dread, as if the whole night was collapsing into that one plate.

qa.q: What did Harsha decide after looking at both columns?
qa.a: That one person would own the fish station on busy nights, with a timer, which fixed the real problem without writing off a good night.

qa.q: How might the new cook see the night if only the fish had been counted?
qa.a: The new cook's fast, clean plating would have gone unnoticed, and the kitchen might have felt like it had failed.

grounding: An adult lists three things that went well beside the one that did not before deciding on a fix, without denying the criticism.

passage: I share a desk with Gopika at the architecture firm, so I saw most of it. On Monday her first presentation to a client came back with a sharp email: the facade was 'too plain for the brief'. She read it, went very still, and then did something I didn't expect. She laid a sheet of tracing paper over her sketchbook and wrote, in her small neat hand: the floor plan they praised; the costs came in under estimate; the client's son loved the courtyard. Then, on the other side: facade too plain. She looked at the two lists for a while. I can't say what she was feeling; her face gave very little away. But after ten minutes she said, 'Harish, can you look at three facade options with me after lunch?' She didn't argue with the email, and she didn't cross out the good lines either.

qa.q: What did the client's email say about the facade?
qa.a: It said the facade was 'too plain for the brief'.

qa.q: What does Gopika's stillness and then her list suggest about how she handled the criticism?
qa.a: It suggests she felt stung but steady, choosing to weigh the criticism next to three real successes before deciding what to do.

qa.q: Why was listing the good points before acting a wise choice?
qa.a: It kept the criticism in proportion without denying it, so her next step was a focused fix, three facade options, rather than panic or defensiveness.

qa.q: How does Harish see Gopika's response?
qa.a: Harish is surprised and impressed that she neither argued with the email nor let it wipe out the good lines.

grounding: A colleague describes an architect listing three things that went well beside one sharp criticism before choosing a fix.

passage:
Monday. A parent's note arrived in Reena's pigeonhole: her Class 4 maths homework was 'too much for small children'. Reena read it three times in the staffroom and felt her face go hot. She'd only been teaching six weeks.
Tuesday. Before deciding anything, she opened her planner and wrote on one side: the class finished the fractions unit on time; three shy children now put up their hands; the head praised her board work. On the other side: homework load, one parent's concern. Noor, the Class 5 teacher, read it over her shoulder. 'Both sides are true,' Noor said. 'Now what?'
Thursday. Reena cut the homework to two short sums a night and wrote to the parent, thanking them for the note. She kept the planner page open on her desk.

qa.q: Which unit did the class finish on time?
qa.a: The class finished the fractions unit on time.

qa.q: How did Reena feel reading the parent's note on Monday?
qa.a: She felt stung and embarrassed, her face going hot, especially being only six weeks into teaching.

qa.q: Why did Reena list three successes before deciding what to do?
qa.a: Seeing the successes beside the one concern kept the criticism in proportion, so she made a fair change to homework without doubting all her teaching.

qa.q: How might the parent feel receiving Reena's reply?
qa.a: The parent would likely feel heard and respected, since Reena thanked them and actually reduced the homework.

grounding: Over a week, a new teacher lists three things going well beside one parent's criticism, then makes a balanced change.

passage:
Hi Kunal,
You asked about the art competition. So, weirdly, my charcoal drawing of Nani's hands won first prize in the district round. Before you get excited: it was luck. The judges probably liked old hands, or they were tired. Anyone could have drawn it; you just copy what you see.
Ms D'Costa said it had 'real feeling' and she wants to put it in the school lobby. Papa framed it. Everyone's making a fuss and it's honestly embarrassing, because I know I can't really draw. Last month's still life was a mess, remember? That's the real me.
Anyway, tell me about your football trials. That's actual talent.
Aadhya

qa.q: What did Aadhya's prize-winning drawing show?
qa.a: It was a charcoal drawing of Nani's hands.

qa.q: Why does Aadhya call the prize luck?
qa.a: Aadhya feels embarrassed by the praise and is used to seeing drawing as a weak spot, so explaining the win away keeps that old self-view comfortable.

qa.q: What could Aadhya try the next time someone praises the drawing?
qa.a: Aadhya could simply say 'thank you' and ask what they liked, instead of listing reasons it doesn't count.

qa.q: How might Ms D'Costa feel if she heard it was 'just luck'?
qa.a: She might feel a little disappointed, since she saw real feeling in the drawing and chose it for the lobby.

grounding: In a letter, a teenager who won a prize for a drawing insists it was luck and that anyone could do it.

passage: Sunaina, stop, you're doing the thing where you say nice stuff. Okay, fine, yes, the mural on the colony wall came out okay. But you have to understand, it's not me. The colony secretary gave us good paint, the wall was smooth, and Ravi Uncle helped with the grid. Anyone with a grid can draw a peacock. Honestly, a little kid could have done it. People keep stopping to take photos and I just want to hide. And then Dadi told the whole building that her Sonali is an artist, and I nearly died. Artist. I got a C in art last term. That's the true number. This was just paint and luck and a smooth wall. Anyway, can we talk about something else? Your exam? Please?

qa.q: Who helped with the grid for the mural?
qa.a: Ravi Uncle helped with the grid.

qa.q: Why does Sonali want to hide when people take photos?
qa.a: Sonali feels embarrassed and uneasy with the praise because it clashes with the idea of being bad at art, so the success gets explained away as paint and luck.

qa.q: What could Sunaina say to help?
qa.a: Sunaina could ask which parts Sonali designed and point to those choices, so the credit lands on the skill, not just the grid and the paint.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel hearing Sonali call it 'paint and luck'?
qa.a: Dadi might feel puzzled and a bit hurt, since she is proud and sees real talent in the mural.

grounding: A teenager praised for a colony mural insists it was luck and that anyone could do it, keeping a low view of their art untouched.

passage:
Monday. Mr Thomas held up Amandeep's pencil sketch of the school banyan tree in art class. 'Look at the shading here.' Amandeep stared at the desk. 'It was a fluke, sir. The pencil was new.'
Wednesday. Jomon leaned over during a free period. 'Can you show me how you did the leaves? Mine look like broccoli.' Amandeep shrugged. 'Anyone can do it. You just scribble.' Jomon tried scribbling. It still looked like broccoli.
Friday. The notice for the inter-school art contest went up with Mr Thomas's handwritten note: Amandeep, please apply. Amandeep read it twice, then walked past to the canteen. Real artists apply to contests, Amandeep thought. Not people who got lucky with a new pencil.

qa.q: What did Amandeep sketch?
qa.a: Amandeep sketched the school banyan tree in pencil.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep walk past the contest notice?
qa.a: Amandeep felt uneasy and unworthy, believing the good sketch was only luck with a new pencil, so applying felt like pretending.

qa.q: What could help Amandeep take the praise seriously?
qa.a: Noticing that Jomon couldn't copy the leaves by scribbling, and asking Mr Thomas what he saw in the shading, would show the skill is real.

qa.q: What might Mr Thomas think when Amandeep doesn't apply?
qa.a: He might feel disappointed and puzzled, since he singled out the shading and wrote a personal note asking Amandeep to apply.

grounding: Over a week, a teenager praised for a sketch calls it a fluke and says anyone can do it, and skips a contest as a result.

passage:
Monday. The economics results went up on the department board, and Salma's name was at the top: 92, the highest in the batch. Binita squealed and hugged her. 'It was an easy paper,' Salma said. 'Everyone did well. It doesn't mean anything.'
Wednesday. Salma got 11 out of 20 in a surprise statistics quiz. She sat on the library steps with the sheet in her lap. 'This is my real level,' she told Binita. 'This is what I actually am.'
Friday. Over chai, Binita put the two papers side by side. 'So the 92 was easy and doesn't count. But an 11 on a surprise quiz is proof. How does that work?' Salma opened her mouth, then closed it. 'It just feels true,' she said finally, and stirred her tea for a long time.

qa.q: What did Salma score in economics?
qa.a: Salma scored 92, the highest in the batch.

qa.q: Why does the 11 feel like 'my real level' to Salma?
qa.a: Salma feels low and doubtful about her ability, so the bad mark fits that self-view and feels true, while the success feels undeserved.

qa.q: What could Salma do to weigh her results fairly?
qa.a: She could use the same rule for both marks, asking whether a top score and a surprise-quiz score each really prove anything about her.

qa.q: How does Binita see Salma's reasoning?
qa.a: Binita sees the double standard clearly and is puzzled and a bit frustrated that her friend discounts a top result.

grounding: Over a week, a student who topped a paper calls it easy and meaningless, then treats a low quiz mark as proof of her real level.

passage: Tushar, you say your first-class result doesn't count because the paper was easy. Your Irawati Maasi used to say exactly that. In my second year of B.Com in Nagpur, I came first in the whole university in cost accounting. Do you know what I told everyone? 'The paper was simple. Anybody could have done it.' That same year I failed one tax internal, and that one, I believed completely. I told myself: that is who you really are, the rest was luck. For three years I lived like that. Every good mark was an accident; every bad one was the truth. Then my professor, Mrs Kulkarni, called me to her cabin with the university merit list. 'Irawati, if the paper was so easy, why did four hundred students score lower than you?' I had no answer. I still think of that question.

qa.q: Which subject did Irawati come first in?
qa.a: She came first in the whole university in cost accounting.

qa.q: Why did Irawati believe the failed internal completely but not the first rank?
qa.a: She felt unsure of herself deep down, so the failure matched that self-doubt and felt like the truth, while success felt like an accident.

qa.q: What turning point in the story challenged Irawati's thinking?
qa.a: Mrs Kulkarni's question, why four hundred students scored lower if the paper was so easy, showed the success was real evidence.

qa.q: How did Mrs Kulkarni see Irawati's result?
qa.a: She saw it as genuine achievement, proved by the merit list, and wanted Irawati to stop dismissing it.

grounding: An aunt recalls how, as a student, she called her top result an easy paper while treating one failure as proof of who she was.

passage: Bhavna had written the semester's Indian history paper after three nights of closing shifts at the bakery near her hostel in Pune, dozing on the bus in between. When the results came, she had the highest mark in the class. Hafsa read it off the notice board twice. 'Topper! On three hours of sleep!' Bhavna shook her head. 'Everyone says the paper was easy. It doesn't count.' 'Who's everyone?' 'People.' That evening, a professor's email said her political science essay needed 'more depth'. Bhavna read it on her bed with the bakery apron still on. 'See,' she said. 'That's the truth. I'm average, and the topper thing was a fluke.' Hafsa sat down beside her. 'So when you do badly, it's because you're average, and when you do well, it's because the paper was easy. You've built a game you can't win.' Bhavna pulled the apron over her face.

qa.q: Where did Bhavna work closing shifts?
qa.a: She worked closing shifts at the bakery near her hostel in Pune.

qa.q: Why does the essay email feel like 'the truth' to Bhavna?
qa.a: She feels tired and doubtful of her ability, so the criticism fits her view of herself as average, while the top mark gets filed as a fluke.

qa.q: What could Bhavna do to break the pattern Hafsa describes?
qa.a: She could judge successes and setbacks by the same rule, for example noting that topping a paper after closing shifts is real evidence of skill.

qa.q: How does Hafsa see Bhavna's reasoning?
qa.a: Hafsa sees an unfair game where every result proves Bhavna is average, and she wants her friend to notice it.

grounding: A student working night shifts tops a paper but calls it easy and meaningless, while treating one critical email as proof she is average.
